abstraction.definition: Leaving out features of a reasoning scenario that do not matter for the question we are studying.

algorithm.definition: A precise, step-by-step procedure that takes an input and produces an output in finitely many steps.

belief-revision.definition: Changing the propositions we accept when we receive new information, including information that conflicts with earlier beliefs.

bivalence.definition: The assumption that each formula has exactly one of the two truth-values, true and false.

boolean-function.definition: A function that takes a fixed number of Boolean values, 0 and 1, as inputs and returns one Boolean value.

cardinality.definition: The number of elements of a set.

classical-logic.definition: The logical framework used in our Boolean and FOL chapters, with bivalent semantics and classical inference principles.

conditional.definition: An if-then statement. In classical logic, A→B is false exactly when A is true and B is false.

conditional-probability.definition: The probability of one claim given another. Formally, Pr(A given B)=Pr(A∧B)/Pr(B), provided Pr(B)>0.

consequence.definition: A conclusion is a logical consequence of premises if every model making the premises true also makes the conclusion true.

contradiction.definition: A formula that is false in every model of the logic under discussion.

countermodel.definition: A model in which all the premises of an inference are true and its conclusion is not true.

deductive-closure.definition: The set of all logical consequences of a set of formulas.

deductive-validity.definition: The impossibility of the premises being true and the conclusion false in the reasoning situations under consideration.

denotation.definition: The object or function assigned to a term symbol by an interpretation.

derivability.definition: The existence of a formal proof of a conclusion from given assumptions, written with ⊢.

designated-value.definition: A truth value counted as acceptable in defining a consequence relation; in K3, only 1 is designated.

disjunction.definition: An or-formula. Classical A∨B is true exactly when at least one disjunct is true, including when both are.

domain.definition: The nonempty set of objects over which an FOL model interprets names, predicates, functions, and quantifiers.

entailment.definition: Another name for semantic consequence, written with ⊨.

equivalence.definition: Two formulas are logically equivalent if they have the same truth-value in every model of the logic.

existential-quantifier.definition: The symbol ∃, used to say that at least one object in the domain satisfies a condition.

expansion.definition: Adding a formula and all its consequences together with the old beliefs: KB+A=Cn(KB∪{A}).

formal-language.definition: A set of finite strings of symbols from an alphabet.

formalization.definition: Representing an expression or inference in a formal language.

formula.definition: An expression formed according to the syntax of a logical language.

free-variable.definition: An occurrence of a variable not governed by a quantifier for that variable.

fuzzy-predicate.definition: A predicate whose extension assigns degrees in [0,1] rather than just membership or nonmembership.

grammar.definition: Rules for generating the expressions of a formal language.

idealization.definition: Representing a situation in a simplified form that need not reproduce all its real features.

inductive-support.definition: Support that premises give a conclusion without guaranteeing it. In probability models, evidence positively supports a conclusion when learning the evidence raises its probability.

inference.definition: A piece of reasoning from premises to a conclusion.

knowledge-base.definition: A collection of represented information used as the starting point for further inference.

logical-validity.definition: Validity that depends on logical form, rather than the particular subject matter of the inference.

material-validity.definition: Correctness that depends on domain-specific meanings, facts, or assumptions; in inductive reasoning, support relative to a particular probability measure.

model.definition: A mathematical representation of a possible reasoning situation; a model of premises makes those premises true.

model-checking.definition: Determining whether a formula is true in a specified model.

modus-ponens.definition: The inference from A → B and A to B.

negation.definition: A not-formula. Classical ¬A is true exactly when A is false.

premise.definition: A statement from which an inference starts.

proof.definition: A chaining of inference rules applied to logical formulas, with assumptions tracked through the derivation.

pseudocode.definition: A precise description of an algorithm written for readers, using programming-like notation without requiring a complete executable program.

semantics.definition: The component of a logical system that specifies interpretations and truth conditions.

substitution.definition: Replacing free occurrences of a variable by a term, while avoiding variable capture.

syntax.definition: The component of a logical system that specifies which expressions are well formed.

tautology.definition: A formula true in every valuation of the propositional logic under discussion.

truth-value.definition: A value assigned to a formula by a semantics, such as 0 or 1 in classical logic.

unification.definition: Finding a substitution that makes two expressions syntactically identical.

universal-quantifier.definition: The symbol ∀, used to say that every object in the domain satisfies a condition.

valuation.definition: A function assigning precisely one Boolean value to every propositional variable of a language.

verification.definition: Checking that a proposed result meets a stated specification; for an argument, checking a proof or a countermodel in the chosen formal setting.

xai.definition: Research into making the behavior and results of AI systems understandable.

conjunction.definition: An and-formula. Classical A∧B is true exactly when both conjuncts are true.

probability.definition: A measure of the chance of an event, given by adding the masses of its outcomes in our finite models.

sample-space.definition: The set of possible outcomes of an experiment, written Ω.

identity.definition: Sameness of objects: a=b is true when the two terms denote the same object.

set.definition: A collection of objects, called its members or elements. Sets are equal when they have exactly the same members.

inductive-validity.definition: In our weak logical sense, conditioning on the premises never lowers the probability of the conclusion, for any distribution giving the premises positive probability.

logic.definition: The discipline that aims to define and understand valid inference.

conclusion.definition: The statement being inferred from the premises of an inference.

validity.definition: In the broad sense used in chapter 1, the premises supporting the conclusion in the way required by the kind of inference under discussion.

inference-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “therefore” or “since”, that signals an inference and helps identify its premises or conclusion.

premise-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “given that”, that signals a premise of an inference.

inference-line.definition: A horizontal line separating the premises above it from the conclusion below it.

inductive-strength.definition: How strongly the premises support a conclusion without guaranteeing it, given the relevant background information.

inductive-validity-in-context.definition: In the sense used in chapter 1, the premises supporting the conclusion strongly enough to justify accepting it, without making it certain.

logical-system.definition: A mathematical model of valid inference, typically comprising syntax, semantics, and proof theory.

proof-theory.definition: The study of formal proofs and the rules by which they are constructed; as a component of a logical system, it models stepwise inference.

logical-law.definition: A general principle of valid inference in a logical system.

counterexample.definition: A case that shows a claim is false. For an inference, it is a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is false.

logical-form.definition: The structure of an expression or inference that matters for logical validity, abstracting from its particular subject matter.

proof-assistant.definition: Software for constructing formal proofs and checking that their steps obey the rules of the proof system.

inference-engine.definition: The part of a reasoning system that applies rules to information in a knowledge base to derive further conclusions.

undecidable-statement.definition: A statement that can neither be proved nor refuted in the theory under discussion.

algorithmic-undecidability.definition: The absence of an algorithm that terminates with the correct yes-or-no answer on every allowed input to a problem.

consistency.definition: A theory is consistent if it does not prove both a statement and its negation.

effective-axiomatization.definition: Specifying the axioms of a theory so that an algorithm can list them all, though the list may be infinite.

conclusion-indicator.definition: A word or phrase, such as “therefore”, that signals the conclusion of an inference.

knowledge-representation-and-reasoning.definition: The study of how to represent information in a form that allows a system to draw conclusions and answer questions.

querying.definition: Asking a database for information by specifying what to retrieve and which conditions it must meet.

system-1.definition: Fast, automatic, intuitive and associative thinking, usually requiring little conscious effort.

system-2.definition: Slow, deliberate and conscious thinking, such as working through a calculation or checking an argument.

set-membership.definition: An object belongs to a set if it is one of its elements, written ∈.

extensional-definition.definition: Specifying a set by listing its elements.

set-abstraction.definition: Specifying a set by a condition its members satisfy, within an intended domain.

alphabet.definition: A set of symbols from which strings of a formal language are formed.

string.definition: A finite sequence of symbols, where order and repetitions matter.

empty-string.definition: The string containing no symbols, often written ε.

kleene-star.definition: For an alphabet Σ, the set Σ* of all finite strings over Σ, including the empty string.

inductive-definition.definition: A definition by initial cases and rules for generating further cases, with nothing else included.

bnf.definition: Notation for grammar rules, using alternatives to specify how expressions can be built.

rewrite-rule.definition: An instruction specifying how one string of symbols may be replaced by another when generating expressions.

parsing.definition: Reconstructing the grammatical structure of a string according to a grammar.

abstract-syntax-tree.definition: A tree representing the structure of an expression while omitting grammatical details such as brackets.

unique-readability.definition: A property of a grammar: every expression it generates has exactly one grammatical structure.

recursion.definition: Defining or carrying out a procedure in terms of further calls to that same procedure.

operator-precedence.definition: A convention specifying which operators bind more tightly when brackets are omitted.

termination.definition: The property that a procedure finishes after finitely many steps on its intended inputs.

algorithm-correctness.definition: An algorithm produces the specified result on its intended inputs; total correctness also requires termination.

propositional-variable.definition: A basic symbol representing a proposition in a propositional language.

logical-operator.definition: A symbol used to form compound expressions, such as negation or conjunction.

biconditional.definition: A connective written ↔ and read “if and only if”; in classical logic it is true when its two parts have the same truth-value.

auxiliary-symbol.definition: A symbol used to mark the grammatical structure of an expression, such as a bracket in propositional logic.

metavariable.definition: A variable in the language used to talk about another language; for example, A standing for any formula of propositional logic.

rooted-tree.definition: A structure of nodes joined by edges, with a designated root and exactly one path from the root to each other node.

numeral.definition: A written expression representing a number; for example, 120 represents the number one hundred and twenty.

ambiguous-grammar.definition: A grammar that generates at least one expression with more than one grammatical structure.

ambiguity.definition: An expression is ambiguous if it has more than one possible reading.

logical-space.definition: The collection of models considered by a semantics.

proposition.definition: In this semantic approach, the set of models in which a formula is true.

subset.definition: S is a subset of T when every member of S belongs to T. Equality is allowed.

intersection.definition: The set of elements belonging to every one of the sets being intersected.

indefeasible.definition: A consequence that cannot be defeated by adding premises while the semantics remains fixed.

defeasible.definition: An inference whose support can be overturned by additional evidence.

probability-function.definition: A measure assigning events probabilities between 0 and 1. In a finite space, outcome masses sum to 1 and event probabilities sum the masses of their outcomes.

fallacy.definition: An invalid pattern of reasoning that may appear correct.

enumerative-induction.definition: Generalizing from observed instances to a universal claim about a population. The universal claim entails its instances, giving weak logical support; the degree of support and the probability of the conclusion depend on the probability function.

event.definition: A set of outcomes in a probability space. In our logical treatment, propositions are events.

log-likelihood-ratio.definition: The logarithm of the ratio of the likelihood of the evidence under a hypothesis to its likelihood under the alternative. Positive values favor the first hypothesis.

sound-argument.definition: A deductively valid argument with true premises, and therefore a true conclusion. Distinct from soundness of a proof system.

inference-schema.definition: A pattern of premises and conclusion with placeholders for expressions of specified grammatical categories.

modus-tollens.definition: The inference from A → B and ¬B to ¬A, valid classically.

disjunctive-syllogism.definition: The inference from A ∨ B and ¬A to B, valid classically.

affirming-the-consequent.definition: The classically invalid pattern from A → B and B to A.

denying-the-antecedent.definition: The classically invalid pattern from A → B and ¬A to ¬B.

affirming-a-disjunct.definition: The invalid pattern from inclusive A ∨ B and A to ¬B; both disjuncts may be true.

likelihood-ratio.definition: The probability of the evidence if a conclusion is true, divided by its probability if the conclusion is false. Ratios above 1 favor the conclusion; ratios below 1 count against it.

material-support.definition: Inductive support relative to a particular probability function and a chosen measure of support.

logical-support.definition: Support that holds across all probability functions on a fixed model space for which conditioning on the premises is defined, using a specified criterion of support.

meaning-postulate.definition: A statement included among the background assumptions to capture a relationship between the meanings of expressions.

probability-raising.definition: Support measured by the conditional probability of the conclusion given the premises minus its unconditional probability. A positive difference favors the conclusion; a negative difference counts against it.

functional-completeness.definition: A collection of truth-functions is truth-functionally complete if every Boolean truth-function of positive finite arity can be expressed using those functions.

boolean-identity.definition: An equation between Boolean expressions that holds for every assignment of Boolean values to its variables.

de-morgan-laws.definition: The identities NOT (X OR Y) = (NOT X) AND (NOT Y) and NOT (X AND Y) = (NOT X) OR (NOT Y).

binary-representation.definition: Positional notation with digits 0 and 1, in which position n, counted from the right starting at 0, has place value 2 to the power n.

adder.definition: A circuit that computes addition on numbers in binary representation.

half-adder.definition: A circuit that adds two bits, returning a sum bit and a carry bit. The sum is XOR of the inputs and the carry is AND of the inputs.

full-adder.definition: A circuit that adds two bits and an incoming carry, returning a sum bit and an outgoing carry.

exclusive-or.definition: The Boolean truth-function XOR, which returns 1 exactly when its two inputs differ.

base-case.definition: A case handled directly by a recursive definition or procedure, without another recursive call.

recursive-case.definition: A case handled by applying the same definition or procedure to smaller parts and combining their results.

set-union.definition: The union S ∪ T contains every object belonging to S or T, including objects belonging to both.

set-difference.definition: The difference S ∖ T contains the members of S that do not belong to T.

set-complement.definition: The complement W ∖ S contains the objects in a specified universe W that do not belong to S.

boolean-evaluation.definition: The extension of a Boolean valuation to all formulas of a propositional language: it keeps the assigned values of variables and interprets ¬, ∧ and ∨ using NOT, AND and OR, respectively.

boolean-value.definition: One of the two values 0 and 1. In logic, they represent false and true, respectively. The Boolean value v(A) of a formula A under a valuation v is determined by the values of its variables and the Boolean functions interpreting its connectives.

boolean-model.definition: A Boolean valuation of the propositional variables of a language, used to represent a possible reasoning situation. It is a model of a formula when that formula has value 1 under the valuation.
